stanzas: Tu scendi dalle stelle, o Re del cielo,
e vieni in una grotta al freddo e al gelo,
e vieni in una grotta al freddo e al gelo.
O Bambino mio divino,
io ti vedo qui tremar;
o Dio beato!
Ahi quanto ti costò l'avermi amato!
Ahi quanto ti costò l'avermi amato!
A te, che sei del mondo il Creatore,
mancâro panni e foco, o mio Signore,
mancâro panni e foco, o mio Signore.
Caro eletto pargoletto,
quanto questa povertà
più m'innamora,
giacché ti fece amor povero ancora,
giacché ti fece amor povero ancora.
Tu lasci il bel gioir del divin seno,
per venir a penar su questo fieno,
per venir a penar su questo fieno.
Dolce amore del mio core,
dove amor ti trasportò?
O Gesù mio,
perché tanto patir? Per amor mio!
perché tanto patir? Per amor mio!
Ma se fu tuo voler il tuo patire,
perché vuoi pianger poi, perché vagire?
perché vuoi pianger poi, perché vagire?
Sposo mio, amato Dio,
mio Gesù, t'intendo sì!
Ah, mio Signore,
tu piangi non per duol, ma per amore,
tu piangi non per duol, ma per amore.
Tu piangi per vederti da me ingrato
dopo sì grande amor, sì poco amato,
dopo sì grande amor, sì poco amato!
O diletto del mio petto,
se già un tempo fu così,
or te sol bramo:
caro non pianger più, ch'io t'amo e t'amo,
caro non pianger più, ch'io t'amo e t'amo.
Tu dormi, Ninno mio, ma intanto il core
non dorme, no, ma veglia a tutte l'ore,
non dorme, no, ma veglia a tutte l'ore.
Deh, mio bello e puro Agnello,
a che pensi? dimmi tu.
O amore immenso,
"Un dì morir per te" – rispondi – "io penso",
"Un dì morir per te" – rispondi – "io penso".
Dunque a morire per me, tu pensi, o Dio
ed altro, fuor di te, amar poss'io?
ed altro, fuor di te, amar poss'io?
O Maria, speranza mia,
s'io poc'amo il tuo Gesù,
non ti sdegnare
amalo tu per me, s'io nol so amare!
amalo tu per me, s'io nol so amare!
orig.credit: Alphonsus Liguori (1744); as quoted in Italian Wikipedia's article

stanzas: You come down from the stars, O King of heaven,
and come into a cave, in the cold and the frost,
and come into a cave, in the cold and the frost.
O my divine Child,
I see you trembling here;
O blessed God!
Ah, how much it cost you to have loved me!
Ah, how much it cost you to have loved me!
To you, who are the Creator of the world,
clothes and fire were lacking, O my Lord,
clothes and fire were lacking, O my Lord.
Dear chosen little child,
how much this poverty
makes me love you the more,
since love made you poor as well,
since love made you poor as well.
You leave the fair joy of the divine bosom
to come and suffer on this hay,
to come and suffer on this hay.
Sweet love of my heart,
where has love carried you?
O my Jesus,
why suffer so much? For love of me!
why suffer so much? For love of me!
But if your suffering was your own will,
why then do you wish to weep, why to wail?
why then do you wish to weep, why to wail?
My spouse, beloved God,
my Jesus, yes, I understand you!
Ah, my Lord,
you weep not for pain, but for love,
you weep not for pain, but for love.
You weep to see yourself by me, the ungrateful one,
after so great a love, so little loved,
after so great a love, so little loved!
O delight of my breast,
if once it was so,
now I long for you alone:
dear one, weep no more, for I love you and love you,
dear one, weep no more, for I love you and love you.
You sleep, my little one, but meanwhile your heart
does not sleep, no, but keeps watch at every hour,
does not sleep, no, but keeps watch at every hour.
Ah, my fair and pure Lamb,
what are you thinking of? Tell me.
O boundless love,
"Of dying for you one day," you answer, "I am thinking",
"Of dying for you one day," you answer, "I am thinking".
So you think of dying for me, O God,
and can I love anything else but you?
and can I love anything else but you?
O Mary, my hope,
if I love your Jesus little,
do not be angry:
love him for me, if I do not know how to love him!
love him for me, if I do not know how to love him!

notes: Line 1.2: grotta, a cave or grotto: in Italian tradition the stable of the Nativity is a cave.
Line 2.2: mancâro, an old form of mancarono, 'were lacking'.
Line 4.4: Sposo mio, 'my spouse' or 'my bridegroom': the soul speaks to Christ as its bridegroom, an old image of Christian devotion.
Lines 5.1-5.2: the Italian word order is free: 'you weep at seeing yourself so little loved by me, ungrateful, after so great a love'.
Line 6.1: Ninno, a Neapolitan word for a baby or little boy.
Line 6.1: il core, 'the heart', here the child's own.
